headline: Walking in Wildlife's Shoes: How One Community Reimagined River Restoration
meta_description: Eighteen volunteers in Somerset experienced the world through animal eyes to understand river pollution's real impact, launching a 30-year restoration campaign.
summary_short: Volunteers became salmon, deer and earthworms to understand how pollution affects wildlife on Somerset's River Tone—then mapped a 30-year plan to restore it.
body:
Eighteen volunteers in Somerset stepped into an extraordinary experiment: they became salmon navigating polluted water, deer confused by altered scents, earthworms overwhelmed by vibrations from farm machinery. The "Risks Beyond Human Eyes" study, led by the University of the West of England and the Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment, trained participants in the physiology and sensory abilities of animals before sending them into the landscape to experience their world firsthand. The goal was radical in its simplicity—to understand not just what wildlife eats or where it lives, but how human activity genuinely harms individual animals' quality of life.

Participant Jake Lawy, who explored the River Tone as an Atlantic salmon, discovered something unexpected: once you see the damage through an animal's perspective, you cannot unsee it. His insight wasn't abstract. He identified concrete changes his community could make—turning off street lights near the river, removing old weirs. Another volunteer, experiencing the area as a deer, realized how a piled earthwork behind a fence had completely altered the animal's sense of direction and safety. These weren't statistics; they were lived moments of vulnerability that sparked recognition.

What emerged from the study became something far larger. The community, inspired by Phil Tovey's background as a Royal Marines Commando, adapted military planning documents to create an unusually serious 30-year campaign for restoring the Tone. Drawing on the Global Nonviolent Action Database, the strategy incorporates increasingly assertive but peaceful tactics if earlier approaches fail. The mapped risks are now available in an online database, and a public webinar on 18 November will share the lessons further. The real victory here is philosophical: a community has reclaimed its river and its animals not as objects to manage, but as neighbours deserving of the same deliberate care we'd offer each other.
quick_facts: 18 volunteers trained to experience animal physiology and senses
Somerset's River Tone chosen as focus for pollution impact study
30-year restoration campaign modeled on military operational planning
University of the West of England led the research
Public webinar scheduled for 18 November to share findings
